metadata.title: GenealogyMagazine, Episode 1: Courthouse Research
metadata.author: GenealogyMagazine
metadata.shortDescription: Have you searched courthouse records in the places where your ancestors lived? Learn the basics about what can be found at the county clerk’s office.
keywords: what does a courthouse researcher do

segments.text: a few years ago Time magazine called
genealogy the second most popular hobby
in the US and the second most visited
category of websites yes
the Internet's where many people begin
their journey into genealogy and for
some it's their only destination except
for a pit stop now and then at the
public library but what about
researching courthouse records into
places where your ancestors lived what
can you find at a county courthouse a
special interest to genealogists our
days probates and vital records that
includes birth certificates marriage
licenses and death certificates these
records are usually found in the county
clerk's office or in the county
recorders office in some places both
final records in the state files are
kept in the office of the probate judge
yet in other places model records are
maintained at town halls or and separate
offices of the county courthouse but
wait there's more
other volumes found in the county
clerk's office buried from courthouse to
courthouse including a registry and
physicians military discharges and
arrest records records I've found to
include a clerk's copy of the 1880
federal census and my great-great grand
uncle's name on a list of confirmed
soldiers with the notation he'd been
killed at Fort Donelson which confirmed
a family story in the basement of an
Alabama courthouse I came across a
newspaper collection dating back to the
1880s and this is how I found an
obituary for my three-times
great-grandmother that alone is enough
to make a genealogist do a happy dance
before you rush off to the courthouse
be prepared you never know what lurks
behind these doors in my experience I
have found most clerks are nice but not
always get out get out come back maybe
this clerk has met one too many
genealogists unlike some public
libraries courthouses are not stacked
with clerks specializing in genealogy
and please don't hold him hostage with
stories about your ancestors I've had
more kisses from clerks than hisses and
smirks by being prepared do your
homework learn as much as possible about
the courthouse know what records are
available and the hours it's opened
do they close for lunch one of my
friends made a long distance trip to a
courthouse only to find that the county
clerk's office has set aside special
days and hours Virginie illogical
inquiries Oh before you go make a list
of documents that you would like to find
have the records in microfilm check
familysearch.org to see what's been
filmed and digitized by the LDS have any
of these records been transcribed for
publication in books periodicals or
online databases transcriptions and
abstracts are extremely helpful but
think of them as guides to records not
substitutes the District Clerk's office
has criminal records as well as civil
suits which is where you'll find
divorced cases these documents are
usually stored in vaults so you'll need
permission for access to these files
except for vinyl records copies usually
cost $1.00 per page and higher if the
copy needs to be certified some
courthouses offer self-service copiers
while others require that all coffees
must be made by clerks
each state mandates the fees for copies
of vital records be prepared to pay $5
to $20 for each certified document often
clerks require that copies be made 15 to
45 minutes before closing time we're
almost out of time this is intended as
an overview of what you can find at a
County Courthouse especially Ana County
Clerk's office in other videos I'll give
research tips and examples of how
courthouse records can help you trace
your family tree
you may go play now
[Music]
you
